CHAIR ( Senator Marielle Smith ): I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 estimates. I'd like to advise an update to the program, which will be distributed. We will be going to lunch 15 minutes early, and we will be extending the time for the Australian National University by 15 minutes, which will be taken from outcome 2. The deputy chair is going to read the opening statement for me.

Senator KOVACIC: I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee has fixed Friday 24 July 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with outcome 2, Higher education, research and international, of the Department of Education, including the Australian Tertiary Education Commission.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

Senator KOVACIC: I have some questions in relation to Startup-HELP loans. Looking at the material provided yesterday, Startup-HELP was a Labor election commitment that was launched by Minister Clare and former minister Husic in 2023. This was a loan program designed to support entrepreneurship by helping young people through Startup Year accelerator programs. Is that a fair description of the purpose of the program?

Ms Joldić : Yes.

Senator KOVACIC: Can you confirm whether the program is continuing at all?

Ms Joldić : As you rightly indicated, the pilot program was designed to support senior university students and research graduates and give them the opportunity to attend accelerated courses to better understand research translation and commercialisation. The very nature of the pilot was to establish whether an idea was viable or not. The government commissioned a review of the program and considered the pilot's effectiveness, and a final decision on the program was made in the context of the budget. I will throw it to my colleagues Ms Morton and Mr Puckett to elaborate on the—

Senator KOVACIC: The continuity?

Ms Joldić : Correct.

Ms Morton : As Ms Joldić has mentioned, a decision was taken in the budget that Startup Year won't be continuing any further. Completions by the people who have taken up a loan will continue. There will be a transition-through arrangement for those people who have accessed the loan, but there will be no new loans offered.

Senator KOVACIC: Will the ongoing expenditure on the measure after this financial year just be on the continuation of those loans that are already in place?

Ms Morton : Yes. My understanding is there's no new ongoing funding for the program. It will simply be for those to be talked through, as it were.

Senator KOVACIC: Is there an expenditure attached to that, and, if so, what is that?

Ms Morton : I might ask Mr Puckett, who's very knowledgeable on this topic, to give you the details of that.

Mr Puckett : The pilot that we're discussing had eight students enrolled altogether. All eight have now concluded their studies, so there will be no further expenditure on the program.

Senator KOVACIC: For the benefit of the Hansard, how much was the average expenditure across those eight people?

Ms Morton : I think the average loan was around $10,000, if I'm correct around that.

Mr Puckett : I don't have the average, but I do have the total across the eight, if that would help? The total loan value was $80,682.

Senator KOVACIC: How many officials worked on the legislation enabling the loan scheme and for how long?

Ms Morton : That was a little before my time, so I may have to take that on notice for you. I don't have that information off the top of my head. It was back in 2023, I think. Can I take that on notice for you?

Senator KOVACIC: Of course. Are you able to tell me, anecdotally, roughly how many people were in the team before the budget decision not to continue?

Ms Morton : I might check with a colleague, if I could.

Senator KOVACIC: Of course.

Ms Morton : Mr Puckett and I have taken it on in the last few weeks, so forgive us if we're filling in some of the blanks with our colleagues.

Senator KOVACIC: Perhaps you could also provide how many officials were responsible for administering the scheme for its duration as well.

Ms Morton : Sure. We're happy to do that.

Senator KOVACIC: You may also have to take on notice the total value of the time that departmental officials spent designing, implementing and now dismantling the scheme.

Ms Morton : Sure. As I've mentioned, we'll need to go back and check that. We'll do our best to get you an answer on that.

Senator KOVACIC: I'm assuming the decision to terminate was a decision of government, or was that based on advice from the department?

Ms Morton : As per usual, our government takes decisions on budget processes based on advice from officials in the budget process.

Senator KOVACIC: Did you have any concerns about the scheme or any insights that you can share with us as to why this scheme failed?

Ms Morton : I think that's going to matters of government consideration. Certainly, as Mr Puckett has already indicated, it was a low take-up, which seems to suggest that perhaps universities had already moved to start thinking about offering similar types of startup courses. It's probably best not to speculate, but that's my—

Senator KOVACIC: Oh, no, I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm curious as to whether any research was done, whether you got feedback from those eight participants, whether you had other applicants or people who inquired and perhaps didn't proceed—some understanding from people in the startup space as to why they didn't take up these loans.

Ms Morton : I think the initial feedback was that it was constructive. I think it was perhaps a case of universities having already started to move to offer a range of startup courses, and there was perhaps just a bit of a timing overlap. That's the main feedback that I can bring to mind at the moment.

Senator KOVACIC: So nothing else of any substance? I'm just concerned. I've run many small businesses and have been in that space, and I know how difficult it is to start them. To have a federal government program that is offering this type of support and to have a total uptake across the country of eight individuals signals to me that there is a bigger problem than perhaps there being other courses available at universities as well.

Ms Morton : I think the intent was solid, and I think that's reflected in, like I said, the university sector already starting to move to offer their own types of courses.

Senator KOVACIC: I understand your commentary about the university sector; I'm trying to understand—

Ms Morton : Industry.

Senator KOVACIC: what the problem was with this scheme. Is your answer that the only issue with this scheme was that there were competitive programs available at universities?

Ms Morton : I think that was one factor. I will have to take on notice any other factors.

Senator KOVACIC: Were the universities offering $10,000 in startup loans as well?

Ms Morton : I think I'd have to take that on notice too, sorry.

Senator KOVACIC: But wouldn't that be a significant driver of—if they weren't offering money and the government were but people were still going to the universities and not to the government, wouldn't that signal that there was a bigger problem with the government program?

Ms Morton : Not necessarily. It depends on the mission of the particular university or provider. We know that there are some very strong providers who are very interested in the early-entry side of their offerings. Others are more interested in the higher research degree. So it's kind of hard to generalise.

Senator KOVACIC: It's not a generalisation; it's just a question, I guess. Minister, I would be interested in your thoughts, briefly, on this, given we have a lot of senators in the room. Have you got any insight for us about what happened here and why we've only had eight people take this up? Clearly there is a problem with design, and clearly it hasn't been able to draw in the entrepreneurs that it had hoped to draw in. Do you see this as a policy failure?

Senator Walsh: The Startup Year program was, as has been discussed, a pilot program. Pilots are always useful for testing approaches, and that is the case with the Startup Year program. Following the pilot, the government has decided not to continue the program. The officials have already spoken to the low take-up in the program. The officials have mentioned the availability of support at universities. It seems likely that the existing range of loans and supports are probably sufficient for these sorts of courses. So, again, it was a pilot program and it won't be continued.

Senator KOVACIC: I would probably suggest otherwise. I don't think there is enough support for startups and small businesses in our country, and to suggest that the only reason that we had an uptake of eight individuals across the country for this program is that there's sufficient support in the ecosystem for small businesses and entrepreneurs is, I think, not accurate. I'm happy to move on, but I would like, perhaps, a consideration of the question that I'm actually asking. Surely there's a bit more to it. Is it that the policy didn't understand the end user—the entrepreneurs and the small businesses? Did the program not work? We can't just point to a competitor taking everybody away.

Senator Walsh: The program was to support students to participate in accelerator programs at universities, so it was a university based program. It had very low take-up. Officials have spoken to some of the reasons for that. There are a range of loan supports available to people—Fee-Help and HECS-HELP loans—and it seems that those loans are sufficient for these courses.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you for your answer. I see it as yet another failure, by government, of young people in our country.

I'm going to ask some questions in relation to the economic accelerator program. I have some documents to table: the documents numbered 10, 11, 11A and 11B. I'd like to ask some questions about program 2.6, Research capacity, and Australia's Economic Accelerator. Now, this is the third set of savings that have been found from Australia's Economic Accelerator. In 2023, through MYEFO, the Albanese Labor government took $46.2 million from the economic accelerator through a reprioritisation measure. In 2025, through MYEFO, the government took a further $73.1 million from that appropriation through another reappropriation measure. This budget, we have reprioritisation of $800 million over the forward estimates and $2.2 billion over the next decade. Is that correct? Is my understanding of those numbers correct?

Mr Cook : I'll just check, with Mr Puckett, the number over the decade.

Senator KOVACIC: I've got $2.2 billion over the next decade.

Mr Puckett : I'm not aware of that number.

Senator KOVACIC: You're not?

Mr Puckett : No.

Senator KOVACIC: Could you check that and confirm that on notice.

Mr Puckett : I'm happy to take it on notice, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: That would be great. On top of that, since this government came to office, we have had reprioritisation measures that cut $56.3 million from 2023-24 and $20.7 million per year ongoing from the Regional Research Collaboration Program in the 2023-24 MYEFO. Is that figure correct?

Mr Cook : I don't have it to hand, but, if you've taken it from budget papers, I'll believe what you're telling me.

Senator KOVACIC: I had a situation yesterday where a couple of them were a little bit out, so I just want to confirm that they are accurate.

Mr Cook : Sure. We'll take it and—

Senator KOVACIC: If they aren't accurate, could you draw my attention to it on notice.

Mr Cook : We will, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: That would be great.

Ms Morton : The regional research program that you mentioned—we're not familiar with that one, so we might just check that one as well for you.

Senator KOVACIC: Of course, that would be wonderful. In each budget since 2022, the government has decided not to extend the Trailblazer Universities Program—which was originally valued at $188.4 million—which means that funding will now end on 1 July. Is that correct? That one is done?

Mr Cook : That's correct, yes. There's no budget from 2026-27 for Trailblazers; that's correct.

Senator KOVACIC: Is the department aware of the other cuts to research spending across the Commonwealth such that, under the most recent science, research and industry budget tables, our investment in R&D will shrink year on year to the point that, by 2028-29—based on the numbers that I have—it will be behind where it was at the start of the decade, and that's before we adjust for inflation? Is that correct?

Ms Morton : The information I have is that, across government, the government has actually increased its investment in research funding. In 2025-26, it provided $15.1 billion, which was a 1.4 per cent increase on $14.9 billion in 2024-25. That was across government. Within the education portfolio, we will be providing $4.2 billion in research funding in 2026-27, and that includes the ARC funding and ANU funding. And then, within the department alone, we're providing around $2.9 billion in funding as well. I'm not sure whether those figures are the same as the ones that you have access to, but there's certainly been an increase across government.

Senator KOVACIC: The figure you're providing is from the SRI tables; is that correct?

Ms Morton : We've got the 2025-26 data, which is the data I've referred to—

Senator KOVACIC: That's from the SRI tables.

Ms Morton : Yes; that is my understanding. The 2026-27 tables are put together by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. They haven't yet put that together.

Senator KOVACIC: The figures I'm providing are also from the SRI tables, from the 2029 figures. If you're able to cross-check that for me, that would be good.

Ms Morton : Yes, we will.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Faruqi.

Senator FARUQI: The Department of Education paid private consultants Nous Group nearly $700,000 for work on the universities accord; is that correct?

Mr Cook : That would have been 24 months ago. We may not have that with us.

Senator FARUQI: It was during 2023, mostly.

Mr Cook : Yes. I know Nous was engaged. I'm sorry; I just don't have the data available to me at the moment. But we can take it on notice to confirm.

Senator FARUQI: I have some numbers, and that's what it comes to; I just wanted to make sure, but if you could confirm that.

You are aware that Nous pretty much has a monopoly in terms of consulting in Australian universities. Their design, advice and change plans, which have seen hundreds of staff jobs, courses and subjects cut—pretty disastrous impacts. Wherever Nous goes, they leave behind a trail of destruction, honestly. Multiple public submissions to the accord process raised concerns about the role of external consultants in the university; I know that because I've seen many of those submissions. Nous was paid to analyse the submissions for the accord; I think that's pretty clear.

Mr Cook : That's correct.

Senator FARUQI: Is it appropriate for consultants to look at submissions which are criticising consultants? I'm asking that question because Nous pretty much said there was not a key issue or theme of the accord process. They pretty much said there was not a big issue with consultants and anything about consultants being a big issue wasn't in the accord.

Mr Cook : We used Nous on the basis that they assisted the accord process with, as you said, summarising the range of submissions. I was originally on the panel but then I moved off the panel when I became secretary, so I don't know what the Nous product was; that's where I'm a bit stuck at the moment.

Senator FARUQI: Nous's assessment was that the role of consultants in university governance was not an important issue for the accord to consider. That's why I ask the question. There were a number of submissions that said it was a big issue. We had an inquiry into university governance here, in this committee, which said that the depth and extent of consultant capture was massive. We know that $1.8 billion a year is spent by universities on consultancies. Is a consultant avoiding saying they are a problem because they want university work?

Ms Mohr : I wasn't here at the time of the accord, so I can't answer the question about how they were engaged in that process. We have already taken that on notice. I think the point you're getting at is around the use of consultants by universities more generally in their—

Senator FARUQI: No, I'm asking about the use of this consultant by the Department of Education.

Ms Mohr : I don't have that answer, but I recognise that the Senate inquiry into governance that this committee undertook raised significant concerns around the use of consultants. That issue is forming part of the work the government is doing to uplift standards across the university sector in respect of governance. The government's committed to making changes to the threshold standards to require providers to provide information about consultancy spending—its purpose, its value and its justification.

Senator FARUQI: I know all of that; I was in the committee that did that. That's not my question. It's alluding to the conflict of interest here. None of you were involved in that in 2023, so you have absolutely no view on whether or not this was an appropriate thing to do. My question is alluding to the conflict of interest here. None of you were involved in that in 2023, so you have absolutely no view on whether this was an appropriate thing to do or not. What happened here was that Nous was informing and supporting the accord process on uni governance and management and then started sucking millions of dollars from universities to help them navigate those reforms. Maybe you could take on notice questions about whether the department implemented any concrete measures for managing conflicts of interests, if the Nous group advised the Department of Education of any measures they were taking to manage conflicts of interest, and what steps the Department of Education took to ensure such measures were actually implemented. Mr Cook : I think they are. We would have covered that in corporate yesterday. I'm sorry, we may have to again take it on notice.

Senator FARUQI: You might take that on notice as well, and the total value of those contracts and the specific work that Nous is contracted for—if they still are—then, I think, show you weren't there at that time, but you should be concerned with this.

Senator FARUQI: I have a couple of questions on managed growth. The managed growth funding is set—we have seen reports recently. It's going to make university entry the toughest it's ever been next year. Under these institution gaps, students may not be able to study their preferred courses at their preferred universities. To get a Commonwealth supported place, students will have to sacrifice—it's pretty clear—their interests and passions and bow down to the Albanese government's priorities. Sure, they might get a place somewhere, but only if they study what that university offers, right? I'm a bit intrigued by what lessons you have learned from the failed and disastrous Job-ready Graduates package, because that's what that tried to do. It tried to force students to do things that they didn't want to do, and that didn't work. Do you think that restricting student choice is going to work?

Mr Cook : I might have our ATEC colleagues assist us with that.

Senator FARUQI: Sure.

Mr Cook : ATEC has been leading some of the work around the managed growth work for the government.

Senator FARUQI: Commissioner Glover, you've been pretty scathing of Job-ready Graduates. To me, this seems like a similar direction of trying to force students to do what they don't want to do. How is this going to work for students?

Prof. Glover : It's great to be back in front of the committee. Thank you, Senator, it's good to see you again after our discussions in the Senate inquiry. I've seen some of the reporting that you're referring to, and I think there are a number of elements of managed growth funding that, in fact, will enable us to be—and we are very confident that there will be more places available in 2027, the first year of managed growth funding, than we have currently. There are sufficient and significant new fully funded places to meet demand—in fact, quite significant demand—that we anticipate building off this year's increased enrolments across the sector in 2027. Importantly, managed growth funding has, as an element of its funding arrangements, the ability to provide places to address demand, essentially demand driven equity so equity students will get a place.

One of the characteristics of admission to Australian universities, which has been the case for decades, is that our students enter essentially through either a tertiary entrance arrangement through one of our tertiary admissions centres, using tertiary rankings, or they go through direct entry arrangements to university, where they apply to universities. Certainly, when students apply, they apply to multiple universities in many cases. Through the preferential ATAR system, they have preferences for courses, and we're very confident students will, by and large, get their first choice. We would encourage students to think about their second and third choices, as they always have done in the preferential ATAR system that operates. Students who apply for direct entry also have an opportunity to apply for direct entry to a number of institutions.

One of the advantages of managed growth funding and the new system is that we will negotiate with universities their entry target for 2027. So we're listening to their strategic intent, their mission as a university, and our ability to provide additional fully funded places above the current commencer load they have in 2026.

Interestingly, in 2026, on current figures, we'd negotiated an increase on 2025 of about 9½ thousand additional full-time-equivalent places in higher education in Australia. This year, on the current data, it looks as if universities will exceed that, and we've negotiated additional places to ensure they can meet that demand. It now looks like in excess of 10,000 additional full-time-equivalent students in the system this year. We are very equipped to meet that—or even more significant growth next year—and fully committed to managing demand driven equity.

In my view, I think we can assure prospective students that the system will grow next year and there are plenty of opportunities for places in Australian universities. My advice to them would be, 'Think carefully about your preferences; think carefully about your first preference; think very carefully, though, about other courses you might like to do as a second or third preference,' as has always been the case. I'm very confident the system will respond to demand next year.

One of the additional elements, as I said, is that, if we see additional demand emerging in the early part of next year, we have the capacity, under managed growth funding, to allocate additional load to universities to meet equity need in the sector, and under the legislation—should the new legislation pass—to provide ATEC with the enabling capability to manage growth in the system, we can, if the system is showing signs of additional demand for equity, apply to the minister for additional places. So I think the mechanisms are there to reassure people that, yes, we'll meet demand, and, yes, the opportunities will be just as strong for students as they have been in the past.

Senator FARUQI: You've given me the overall picture, but the question still remains: if someone wants to go to UNSW for a particular course, it's firstly going to create more competition, so ATARs are going to rise. We know that's pretty clear. If someone wants to do a course at the University of New South Wales and there are only so many places—which, with managed growth funding, have been cut back in certain universities or restricted compared to others; there's growth in other universities—they will not get that. Then you will negotiate with that university to increase those places? It's pretty clear that, if there are barriers for students who want to go to a certain university to do a certain course and the place is not there, they will either have to go somewhere else or not do that course. That's pretty clear, right?

Prof. Glover : What I will say is that, having been involved in providing advice on commencer load for 2026 with universities, we negotiated their load envelope. So they accepted, based on their estimated projected load, the places they would need. Many courses have ATAR variations from year to year. ATARs occasionally go up and occasionally go down. It depends on demand. Demand does vary in courses from year to year. I'm very confident that universities will have sufficient places next year to not see dramatic changes in ATARS. I think it's very reassuring, if we take the Sydney example, that we have great universities available for students in the Sydney basin with opportunities to study if they don't happen to get into their university of first choice. But I think overwhelmingly students will; I'm very confident of that. Most importantly, we're putting significant new fully funded places into commencer load next year.

Senator FARUQI: I do know that. My question is quite different, but thank you for responding. I have questions on the Antisemitism Education Taskforce reference group and the Commonwealth Research Grants Working Group. Prof. Roessner : [Inaudible] to announce those which are not under due diligence within the timeframe and then proceed with due diligence as we need to.

Senator FARUQI: But you are doing preliminary stuff still to reduce the time for those as well. Okay.

I wanted to get an update on the workings of the Commonwealth Research Grants Working Group. Professor Shergold, I think you are also the Chair of the Commonwealth Research Grants Working Group.

Senator FARUQI: So the framework will consider all forms of hate and racism and not just antisemitism.

Prof. Shergold : Correct.

Senator FARUQI: When will you be providing this framework for the ARC to guide funding decisions for other organisations?

Senator FARUQI: And will the criticism of Israel be deemed to be inconsistent with those hate speech laws? Have you gone into that detail yet?

That would apply to the topics of the research, the researchers or, indeed, the partners. But we haven't gone into this type of—it will not go down to that level. Senator FARUQI: I'm presuming you will take this on notice, but the Australian Research Council awarded Monash University research this year around $1.7 million to map the ageing primate brain. Would you have information on individual grants like that? Can that be easily looked up?

Prof. Shergold : I think you asked us a similar question about non-human primates last time, and we've answered that one on notice. I think there were six that we had identified for you, and we can do the same again.

Senator FARUQI: I'm not asking if you police it. Do you have any oversight? You don't have any idea of whether they are breaching these codes?

Prof. Shergold : Senator, this was the reason I wanted to make the opening statement, so I shall do it now. It is incorrect to say we do not have any monitoring or oversight. What the board does when grants come forward is—we don't second-guess whether or not that's appropriate. We set high store by the integrity of the process. The integrity of the process means that the universities are fulfilling their important role in making sure, for example, that all the ethics approvals are in place.

Senator FARUQI: I might put some other questions on notice. Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator O'Sullivan.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Can you explain why an applicant seeking funding to bring this person to Australia would've been approved?

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Take the question on notice—yes. In doing so, can you explain why, after 7 October 2023, a project seeking funding to bring Erakat to Australia would not have been cancelled?

Senator O'SULLIVAN: Do you know whether you or Macquarie, during the suspension, considered national security matters? For example, Dr Abdel-Fattah's links with institutions overseas that have links to convicted terrorists and her seeking funding to bring Ms Erakat to Australia—were they ever considerations?

Prof. Shergold : I'm not sure of that. At the moment, Senator, I'm just accepting your descriptions of what this is—

Prof. Shergold : It can do.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: It's DE260100761. The description is:

Guided by Yolngu and Gumbaynggirr Custodians, Dr Lara Daley's project will help shape culturally respectful and environmentally responsible space exploration.

Learning from songlines, creation stories and deep cultural connections between people and sky Country, the research will develop intercultural guidelines to help inform space policy, public education and industry practice. The project aims to broaden Australia's understanding of space by recognising long-held Indigenous knowledge systems and their relevance to sustainable human activity beyond Earth.

My question relates to this and whether the ARC can outline how the national interest test for this project satisfied the requirement to demonstrate a benefit to Australia beyond the academic community, as required under the National Competitive Grants Program.

Prof. Shergold : Again, I have to fall back on telling you that we have a peer review process. The details of that peer review process are now set out on our website, and it's in detail. Chair, I'm very happy to make that available to all members of this group in future, but it is essentially based upon a peer review process which was undertaken, and I am assured that the process overall that was undertaken had significant integrity.

I can't sit here and have a discussion with you about whether you or I would have funded that process. It is an impossible way to allocate a billion dollars of taxpayers' money in grants. The only way you can do that is by having a systematic peer review process with experts in the field making recommendations. And then I have to rely on that process and make sure I am satisfied with those processes in order then to approve the decision with the rest of the board. But we cannot—you would understand this: it would be inconceivable for a board to sit around a table each year and look at thousands of applications and see the recommendations that are made to us and go through each of those in turn. What I can do is to give myself and you assurance that the processes undertaken for a peer review process were performed with the utmost integrity.

Prof. Roessner : There are assessment criteria around feasibility and benefit, which the assessors have to take into consideration. This is a DECRA application—very highly competitive. One in 10 might be successful. That would have been a very rigorous process to determine the value of that research, because the assessors have, of course, access to the full proposal, whereas the public has access only to the 100-word summary.

Prof. Shergold : It does mean you have to take into account the public interest, yes.

Senator O'SULLIVAN: We've got two minutes. The motivation for my question is to understand—you mentioned 'competitive'. There are obviously lots of competing applications, and decisions are made. Given the limited availability of research funds—while it is collectively a sizeable amount—for each project, taxpayers need to ensure value for money, and, of course, I understand one of the guiding principles is that it has a benefit beyond just the academic community. Prof. Shergold : Let me, again, be clear. The fact that it is in the national or the public interest doesn't mean the research project has commercial applications. There's a large amount of blue-sky science research that wouldn't fit that category. One of the things that would have been taken into account here, I am certain, would have been in terms of the national interest in terms of Australian culture.
